newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Political violence kills 149 in Karachi in 4 month.
newsitem.headline: Political violence kills 149 in Karachi in 4 month.

text.p: Karachi's police chief said on Friday that 149 people had been killed in political violence in the Pakistani city in the last four months.
"Since March 1, 149 people were killed in terrorism-related cases, while 127 people died in (cases linked to) personal enmity," Mohammad Iqbal told reporters.
He gave no death toll for the whole year.
In the latest incident, ambulance workers collected the bullet-riddled body of an unidentified yongster from the volatile Malir area earlier on Friday.
Iqbal said police were trying to control what he called an "alarming situation" and curb the surge of killings.
Political violence has risen in Karachi since Pakistan's February 3 election, with the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) locked in conflict with the breakaway MQM-Haqiqi faction.
The MQM, which endured a tough crackdown during Benazir Bhutto's 1993-96 government, blames security agencies as well as MQM-Haqiqi for the renewed violence in the southern port.
MQM-Haqiqi denies the charge and accuses MQM militants of killing its party workers to monopolise power.
The MQM, which joined a provincial coalition government after the elections, speaks for Urdu-speaking people who migrated from India at Partition in 1947 and their descendants.

Iqbal said 29 MQM and 26 MQM-Haqiqi members had been killed in the past four months. The dead also included three from the ruling Pakistan Muslim League and one from a splinter faction of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, led by Ghinwa Bhutto since her husband Murtaza was killed by police in Karachi in September.
Seven policemen and 80 people, including an undisclosed number of police informers, had also been killed, Iqbal said.
More than 500 people died in political, ethnic and sectarian violence in Karachi in 1996 and more than 2,000 in 1995.
At a meeting with provincial chief ministers in Islamabad on Thursday, Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif asked Sindh chief minister Liaquat Jatoi to restore order in Karachi, an official said.
"The law and order problem in Karachi is hampering the government's efforts for the revival of the country's ailing economy," added the official, who asked not to be named.
